species.ident: A very small diving duck with a large head. Males are white with a black back and a large white patch across the back of an iridescent purple-green head; females are gray-brown with an oval white cheek patch.
species.nat: Dives for aquatic invertebrates and seeds, often in small groups, staying under for about 12 seconds at a time. Nests in old flicker holes near lakes in the boreal forest and in a few northern California mountain lakes.
species.dist: A common winter visitor from October to April on bays, estuaries, lakes and ponds statewide. A small number breed in the Cascades and northern Sierra Nevada.
species.find: Lake Merced, Crissy Field marsh, the Golden Gate Park lakes, Heron's Head Park and sheltered Bay coves.
species.photo: The male's head only shows purple and green when the sun is behind you and the bird turns toward the light; in other light it reads as black. Expose for the white flanks. Because the birds dive constantly, pick one, time the dives and be ready as it surfaces. Shoot from as close to water level as the shore allows.

species.cons: Mount Pinos race only: State candidate (2026)

species.ident: A stocky, medium-sized hummingbird, about 10 cm long, green above and gray below. Adult males have an iridescent rose-magenta crown and throat that flashes or goes black depending on the angle of the light; females show a small central patch of rose spots on the throat. Compare Allen's and Rufous Hummingbirds, which show rufous on the flanks and tail, and Costa's, whose male gorget is violet with long flared corners.
species.nat: Feeds on nectar and on small insects taken in flight or from spider webs. Males hold song perches and perform steep display dives that end in an explosive chirp made by the tail feathers. Nesting begins very early, often in December or January on the coast. Most birds are resident, with some local movement after breeding.
species.dist: Year-round resident through coastal and lowland California, the Central Valley and the foothills, and common in cities wherever flowering plants and feeders are available. Its range expanded during the twentieth century along with ornamental planting.
species.find: Present all year in almost any San Francisco garden or park. Reliable places include the San Francisco Botanical Garden and the rest of Golden Gate Park, the Presidio, Fort Mason community garden and Heron's Head Park.
species.photo: Males return to the same exposed twig again and again, so pick a perch with a clean, distant background and wait at the 2.4 m minimum focus distance or beyond. Position yourself with the sun behind you to light the gorget. For perched birds 1/500 s is enough; to freeze the wings in a hover use 1/3200 s or faster with Auto ISO, and expect f/8 at 600 mm to push ISO high outside bright light. Bird subject detection with AF-C and a small zone works well.

species.cons: Federal Endangered; State Endangered or Threatened (all three California races)

species.ident: A stocky, all-black shorebird with a long, bright red-orange bill, yellow eye with a red ring, and pale pink legs. Loud piping whistles carry over the surf. Unmistakable in the region.
species.nat: Lives on wave-washed rocky shore, prying limpets and mussels from the rocks. Pairs hold territories for many years and lay their eggs in a scrape just above the high tide line. The population is small and vulnerable to disturbance.
species.dist: Resident on rocky coast and offshore rocks along the whole California coast, becoming scarce south of Point Conception.
species.find: Rocky shoreline at Lands End, Sutro Baths, Fort Point, Seal Rocks, Pillar Point and the Marin Headlands. Stay well back from birds on territory between April and August.
species.photo: A black bird on dark rock in bright surf is a hard exposure. Meter for the bird, add +1/3 to +2/3 stop and let the foam run bright, or wait for overcast light. The red bill is the focal point, so place focus on the eye and bill. Low tide brings birds onto exposed mussel beds within range of 600 mm.

species.ident: A large, cinnamon-buff shorebird with a very long, slightly upturned bill that is pink at the base and dark at the tip. Shows cinnamon underwings in flight. Long-billed Curlew is similar in color but has a long, strongly downcurved bill.
species.nat: Probes deeply into mud and wet sand for worms, clams and crabs, often with the whole head underwater. Roosts in tight flocks at high tide. Breeds on the northern Great Plains.
species.dist: Common on coastal mudflats, estuaries and beaches from July to May; some non-breeding birds stay through summer. San Francisco Bay is one of its most important wintering sites.
species.find: Mudflats at Heron's Head Park, Crissy Field, Arrowhead Marsh in Oakland, Palo Alto Baylands, Bolinas Lagoon and Pillar Point.
species.photo: Check a tide table. A rising tide pushes feeding birds toward the shoreline and concentrates them at roosts. Warm early or late light suits the cinnamon plumage. Leave room in the frame for the bill, and try a group in a line with the nearest bird in focus.

species.ident: A small, plump sandpiper with a black bill and legs. In winter it is very pale gray above and white below, often with a dark mark at the bend of the wing; breeding birds are rufous on the head and breast. Lacks a hind toe.
species.nat: Runs up and down the beach with the waves, probing wet sand for small crustaceans and worms. Breeds in the high Arctic and migrates as far as southern South America.
species.dist: A common migrant and winter visitor on sandy beaches along the whole coast from late July to May; a few non-breeders remain in summer.
species.find: Ocean Beach, Fort Funston, Baker Beach, Crissy Field beach and the outer coast beaches of San Mateo and Marin counties.
species.photo: Lie down on the sand. A lens a few centimeters above the beach turns foreground and background into smooth color and puts you at the bird's eye level. Stay put and let the flock work toward you. Use 1/2000 s for running birds, and add +1/3 to +2/3 stop because bright sand and foam cause underexposure.

species.ident: A large, stocky, gray-brown shorebird with a straight, thick bill and blue-gray legs. Plain at rest, but in flight reveals a bold black-and-white wing pattern. Greater Yellowlegs is slimmer with bright yellow legs; Marbled Godwit is cinnamon-buff with a long upturned bill.
species.nat: Feeds on mudflats, beaches and rocky shore on crabs, worms and small mollusks. Loud ringing calls. The western population breeds on interior marshes and prairies and winters on the coast.
species.dist: Common on the coast from July to April, with non-breeders through the summer. Breeds in northeastern California in the Modoc Plateau and Great Basin wetlands.
species.find: Tidal flats and beaches: Crissy Field, Heron's Head Park, Ocean Beach, India Basin and the Bay shoreline south to the Palo Alto Baylands.
species.photo: The wing pattern is the picture. Watch for a bird that stretches or lifts its wings on landing, and shoot at 1/2500 s. On mudflats, work a falling tide in early light and stay low. Tolerant of people on busy beaches.

species.ident: A large gull with a dark slate-gray back, white head that stays unstreaked in winter, heavy yellow bill with a red spot and pink legs. Takes four years to reach adult plumage. California Gull is smaller with yellow-green legs and a paler back; Glaucous-winged Gull is paler with gray wingtips.
species.nat: An opportunistic feeder on fish, marine invertebrates, carrion and refuse, and a predator of seabird eggs and chicks. Nests on islands, sea stacks, piers and rooftops. Hybridizes with Glaucous-winged Gull from northern California northward.
species.dist: Resident along the entire coast and on San Francisco Bay; rarely seen far inland. A large share of the world population nests on the Farallon Islands.
species.find: Everywhere on the waterfront: Ocean Beach, Crissy Field, Fisherman's Wharf, Lands End and Alcatraz.
species.photo: Tame and always available, which makes it the best subject for practicing exposure and flight tracking before more difficult birds. White head and dark back together need careful exposure; protect the whites. Try slower shutter speeds, around 1/60 s, for panning blurs of birds in flight along the surf.

species.ident: A large, all-dark marine cormorant with a buffy patch at the base of the bill. Breeding adults show a vivid cobalt-blue throat pouch and fine white plumes on the head and back. Double-crested Cormorant has an orange-yellow throat; Pelagic Cormorant is slimmer with a thin neck and, in spring, white flank patches.
species.nat: Dives for fish over rocky bottom and kelp, often in large flocks. Nests in dense colonies on offshore rocks and islands. Strictly coastal.
species.dist: Resident along the whole California coast, with major colonies on the Farallon Islands and on rocks and headlands from Point Reyes to the Channel Islands.
species.find: Rocks off Lands End, the Cliff House and Seal Rocks, the Golden Gate, Alcatraz and Pillar Point.
species.photo: Usually distant on offshore rocks, where 600 mm and a tripod or monopod help. Black plumage needs +1/3 to +2/3 stop to hold feather detail; shooting in morning light from the east brings out the blue throat in spring. Heat shimmer over water softens long-distance frames by midday.

species.ident: A large, dark cormorant with a hooked bill and orange-yellow skin on the face and throat. Juveniles are brown with a pale breast. Flies with a kink in the neck and often perches with wings spread to dry.
species.nat: Dives for fish in fresh and salt water. Nests colonially in trees, on bridges and transmission towers and on islands. The only cormorant regularly found inland.
species.dist: Resident on the coast, on San Francisco Bay and on large inland lakes and rivers; breeds locally throughout the state.
species.find: Lake Merced, the Golden Gate Park lakes, Crissy Field, the Bay shoreline and bridge structures.
species.photo: The wing-drying pose on a piling is the standard image; look for a side-lit bird against dark water and expose to keep texture in the black plumage. Closer than the marine cormorants, so 400 mm is often enough. The turquoise eye is worth a tight portrait at 600 mm.

species.ident: A very large, dark seabird with a long bill and pouch, gray-brown body and, in adults, a white to yellowish head. Juveniles are brown with a pale belly. American White Pelican is white with black flight feathers and does not plunge-dive.
species.nat: Feeds by plunge-diving from the air onto schooling fish such as anchovies and sardines. Flies in lines low over the swells. Nests on islands off southern California and Mexico and disperses north after breeding.
species.dist: Present on the coast all year, with the largest numbers in central and northern California from summer through autumn. Breeds on the Channel Islands. The species recovered after DDT was banned and was removed from the federal endangered list in 2009.
species.find: Crissy Field and the Golden Gate, Ocean Beach, Lands End, Fort Point, the Cliff House and Pillar Point Harbor.
species.photo: Large and predictable in flight, which makes it a good subject for learning birds in flight. Lines of birds pass close to shore at Fort Point and along the bluffs; track with AF-C at 1/2000 s. At 600 mm a close pelican overfills the frame, so zoom out to 200-300 mm. For dives, follow one circling bird and begin the burst as it folds its wings.

species.ident: A slender, medium-sized white heron with a thin black bill, yellow skin in front of the eye, black legs and bright yellow feet. Great Egret is much larger with a yellow bill and black feet.
species.nat: An active feeder that runs through the shallows, stirs the bottom with its feet and strikes at small fish and crustaceans. Grows long, lacy plumes in the breeding season. Nests colonially, often with night herons.
species.dist: Resident on the coast and in the Central Valley, around San Francisco Bay and at the Salton Sea; more widespread in the interior in summer.
species.find: Tidal shallows and marsh channels: Crissy Field marsh, Heron's Head Park, India Basin, Lake Merced and the Palo Alto Baylands.
species.photo: White plumage clips quickly in sun. Use -2/3 to -1 stop of compensation, check the histogram and prefer early or late light. Feeding birds are energetic, so 1/2000 s keeps the strike and the flying water sharp. Dark water behind the bird gives the strongest contrast.

species.ident: A stocky, short-necked heron. Adults have a black cap and back, gray wings, white underparts and red eyes; juveniles are brown with white spots and streaks. Usually seen hunched and motionless.
species.nat: Feeds mainly at dusk and through the night on fish, crustaceans and other small animals, and roosts by day in trees or reeds. Nests in colonies.
species.dist: Resident in lowland California around marshes, lakes and harbors, with some withdrawal from colder interior areas in winter.
species.find: Day roosts and feeding edges at Lake Merced, the Golden Gate Park lakes, the Palace of Fine Arts lagoon and the Lake Merritt area in Oakland. A colony nests on Alcatraz.
species.photo: Roosting birds sit still in shade, which allows slow shutter speeds: with lens and body stabilization 1/125 s at 600 mm is practical from a braced position. Focus on the red eye. The best activity is in the last half hour of daylight, when ISO 6400 and above will be needed.

species.ident: A tall, all-white heron with a long S-shaped neck, yellow bill and black legs and feet. In breeding condition the skin in front of the eye turns green and long plumes grow from the back.
species.nat: Hunts by standing still or walking slowly in shallow water and fields, taking fish, frogs and small mammals. Nests colonially in trees. Hunted heavily for its plumes around 1900, and its recovery became an early success of the bird protection movement.
species.dist: Resident near water through lowland California, with the largest numbers on the coast, in the Central Valley and in the Imperial Valley.
species.find: Crissy Field marsh, Lake Merced, Heron's Head Park and Golden Gate Park. Audubon Canyon Ranch at Bolinas Lagoon is known for its heronry; check current access before visiting.
species.photo: Expose for the whites, with -2/3 to -1 stop in sun. The size allows shooting at 150-300 mm, which is useful for including habitat. Backlit birds in breeding plumes against a dark background are a classic image early or late in the day.

species.ident: The largest North American heron, about 1.2 m tall, blue-gray with a white face, black plume behind the eye and a heavy yellowish bill. Flies with slow wingbeats and the neck folded back. Great Egret is all white.
species.nat: Stands motionless or wades slowly, striking at fish, frogs and crabs, and also hunts gophers in fields. Nests colonially in tall trees, with courtship and nest building from late winter.
species.dist: Resident statewide near water of any kind, from tidal marsh to mountain lakes.
species.find: Lake Merced, Crissy Field marsh, Heron's Head Park and the Golden Gate Park lakes. A nesting colony has used the trees at Blue Heron Lake (formerly Stow Lake) for many years; view it from the path without approaching the nest trees.
species.photo: Large and patient, so it often fills the frame at 300-400 mm; zoom out to leave room for the bill and a reflection. For the strike, pre-focus on the head and shoot a burst at 1/2000 s when the neck coils. A low position at the water's edge gives the cleanest background.

species.ident: A crow-sized hawk with short rounded wings and a long, rounded tail with a white tip. Adults are blue-gray above with a dark cap and fine rufous barring below; juveniles are brown above with thin dark streaks on a whitish breast. Sharp-shinned Hawk is smaller with a square-tipped tail and a smaller head.
species.nat: A bird hunter that takes doves, robins, starlings and jays in fast, low pursuit through trees and gardens. Nests in tall trees and has become a regular breeding bird in cities.
species.dist: Resident through most of California in woodland, riparian forest and towns; additional birds arrive from the north in winter.
species.find: Wooded parks and neighborhoods with street trees: Golden Gate Park, the Presidio, Dolores Park, Bernal Heights and Glen Canyon Park.
species.photo: Most sightings are brief. The dependable situations are birds on a kill or perched near a nest, where they may sit for some time; keep a respectful distance from active nests. Have the camera set for action before you need it: AF-C, bird detection, 1/2500 s and Auto ISO.

species.ident: A medium-sized forest hawk. California adults are richly colored, with rufous-orange barring below, rufous shoulders, black-and-white checkered wings and a black tail with narrow white bands. In flight shows translucent pale crescents near the wingtips. The call is a loud, repeated 'kee-yar'.
species.nat: Hunts from perches inside and at the edge of woodland for small mammals, frogs, lizards and large insects. Vocal, especially in late winter and spring. Nests in tall trees, including eucalyptus.
species.dist: Resident west of the Sierra Nevada in riparian and oak woodland and in wooded suburbs. The California population is isolated from the eastern one and has expanded with the planting of trees in towns.
species.find: Wooded parks: Golden Gate Park, the Presidio, Stern Grove, Glen Canyon Park and McLaren Park.
species.photo: Often perches lower and allows a closer approach than Red-tailed Hawk, typically on a shaded branch at the woodland edge. Expect ISO 1600-6400 under the canopy. Follow the call to find the bird, then move slowly and stop well short; a hawk that keeps looking at you is about to leave.

species.ident: A large, broad-winged hawk. Most adults have a rufous tail, a pale chest with a band of dark streaks across the belly, and dark marks on the leading edge of the underwing. Plumage is variable and dark morphs occur. Juveniles have a finely barred brown tail. Red-shouldered Hawk is smaller with a banded tail and pale crescents near the wingtips.
species.nat: Soars over open country and perches on poles and tall trees watching for rodents, rabbits and snakes. Often hangs motionless on the wind along coastal bluffs. Pairs build large stick nests high in trees or on cliffs.
species.dist: Resident throughout California in nearly every open habitat. Numbers rise in autumn and winter with migrants.
species.find: Seen over most of the city. Good places include the Presidio, Lands End, Bernal Hill, Fort Funston and Mount Davidson. Hawk Hill in the Marin Headlands concentrates migrating raptors from September to November.
species.photo: For birds in flight use AF-C with bird detection, 1/2000 s or faster, and +2/3 to +1 stop of compensation against bright sky to hold detail in the underside. Coastal bluffs with onshore wind bring birds to eye level. A perched bird usually defecates and leans forward just before taking off, which is the cue to start a burst.

species.ident: A small, upright flycatcher, sooty black with a sharply defined white belly, that pumps its tail constantly. Juveniles show cinnamon wingbars. No similar species in the region.
species.nat: Hunts from low perches near water, sallying out for flying insects and returning to the same spot. Builds a mud nest under bridges, eaves and culverts. Resident and often solitary outside the breeding season.
species.dist: Resident through lowland California west of the deserts and along the Colorado River, almost always near water: streams, ponds, shorelines and irrigated parks.
species.find: Common around water and buildings: Crissy Field, Lake Merced, Heron's Head Park, the Golden Gate Park lakes and Mission Creek.
species.photo: A dependable subject because it returns to the same perch after each sally; pre-focus on the perch for landing shots at 1/2500 s. The black-and-white plumage exceeds the sensor's range in hard sun, so overcast or early light is better. Expose to keep detail in the white belly.

species.cons: State Endangered (both California races); Federal Endangered (Least race)
San Clemente Island race only: Federal Endangered

species.ident: A long-tailed, crestless jay, blue on the head, wings and tail with a gray-brown back, white eyebrow and a pale throat bordered by a partial blue necklace. Steller's Jay is darker with a prominent crest and no white below.
species.nat: Omnivorous and bold. In autumn it buries thousands of acorns, many of which are never retrieved, making it an important planter of oaks. Pairs hold territories year-round and nest in dense shrubs or low trees.
species.dist: Resident west of the Sierra Nevada crest in oak woodland, chaparral and suburbs, from the Oregon border to Baja California. Replaced in the Great Basin and desert ranges by Woodhouse's Scrub-Jay.
species.find: Common in neighborhoods and parks with oaks or shrubs: Golden Gate Park, the Presidio, Glen Canyon Park, Bernal Hill, and East Bay regional parks such as Tilden.
species.photo: Approachable and often perched in the open on fence posts and shrub tops, so 300-400 mm is frequently enough. Blue plumage looks best in soft or overcast light; in sun, underexpose by a third of a stop to hold detail in the pale throat. In autumn, birds carrying acorns make good behavior shots at 1/1600 s.

species.ident: A small chickadee with a dark brown cap, black bib, white cheeks and a rich chestnut back. Birds on the central California coast have mostly gray flanks. Mountain Chickadee has a white eyebrow and gray back.
species.nat: Active and acrobatic, gleaning insects and seeds from foliage, often hanging upside down. Joins mixed flocks with kinglets, nuthatches and creepers outside the breeding season. Nests in tree cavities lined with fur and moss.
species.dist: Resident in humid coastal conifer forest from the Oregon border to San Luis Obispo County and in parts of the Sierra Nevada, and now also in planted pines, eucalyptus and suburban gardens around the Bay.
species.find: Any wooded park: Golden Gate Park, the Presidio, Mount Sutro, Mount Davidson and the Marin and East Bay hills.
species.photo: Small, fast and usually in shade. Use 1/1600 s or faster and accept ISO 3200-6400; a sharp, noisy frame is more useful than a blurred clean one. Burst shooting helps because the bird changes position several times a second. Birds come lower at water and at feeders.

species.ident: A tiny, short-tailed nuthatch with a gray-brown cap that reaches the eye, blue-gray back and buffy underparts. Highly vocal, with constant high piping calls. Red-breasted Nuthatch has a black eye-line and white eyebrow.
species.nat: Travels in noisy family groups through the outer branches and cones of pines, feeding on insects and pine seeds. A cooperative breeder, with young from earlier broods helping at the nest. Groups roost together in cavities.
species.dist: Resident in pine forest: Monterey and bishop pine on the coast, and ponderosa and Jeffrey pine in the mountains. Common in planted pines and cypress in San Francisco.
species.find: Pine and cypress stands in the Presidio, Golden Gate Park, Lincoln Park and Lands End, and Sutro Heights.
species.photo: Stays high in the canopy, so 600 mm is usually needed, often pointing steeply up against bright sky; add +2/3 to +1 stop of exposure compensation. Look for trees on a slope where you can stand level with the crown, or for birds visiting nest holes in spring, which are often lower.

species.ident: A large thrush, gray-brown above with a brick-orange breast, white crescents around the eye and a yellow bill. Juveniles are spotted below. Varied Thrush has an orange eyebrow, orange wingbars and a dark breast band.
species.nat: Runs and pauses on lawns hunting earthworms, and takes large quantities of berries in autumn and winter. Sings a rich caroling song from before dawn. Builds a mud-reinforced cup nest.
species.dist: Breeds widely in forest, parks and gardens through most of California; large flocks from the north and the mountains winter in the lowlands, with numbers varying from year to year with the berry crop.
species.find: Lawns and wooded parks throughout the city: Golden Gate Park, the Presidio parade grounds, Stern Grove and Dolores Park. Winter flocks gather at fruiting trees.
species.photo: Lawn-feeding birds are easy to work at eye level from a low position. Winter flocks at toyon, pyracantha or cotoneaster offer behavior shots of birds taking berries; use 1/1600 s and a burst for the moment a berry is tossed back.

species.ident: A small sparrow with a pale pink bill and white outer tail feathers that flash in flight. The 'Oregon' form found in California has a dark hood (black in males, gray in females), brown back and pinkish-buff flanks.
species.nat: Forages on the ground in small flocks for seeds, and takes insects in the breeding season. Nests on or near the ground, often on a sheltered bank. Flocks swell in winter with birds from the mountains and from farther north.
species.dist: Breeds in conifer and mixed forest through the mountains and along the coast, and has become a common breeding bird in urban parks and campuses. Widespread at lower elevations in winter.
species.find: Common in the Presidio, Golden Gate Park, Mount Sutro, Stern Grove and most wooded neighborhoods.
species.photo: Feeds in shade under trees, so plan for high ISO or wait for birds that move to the sunlit edge of a path. Shoot from ground level. Flocks flush as a group; staying still and letting them work toward you gives closer, calmer frames than approaching.

species.ident: A large, gray-breasted sparrow with bold black and white crown stripes and a yellowish to orange-pink bill; first-winter birds have brown and tan stripes instead. Golden-crowned Sparrow has a yellow forecrown bordered in black and a dusky bill.
species.nat: Feeds on the ground on seeds, buds and insects, usually close to shrub cover. The resident coastal 'Nuttall's' form has been studied for decades for its local song dialects.
species.dist: The Nuttall's form is resident in the coastal fog belt from Mendocino to Santa Barbara County. Other forms breed in the high Sierra Nevada, and migrants from the north are abundant across lowland California from late September to April.
species.find: Coastal scrub and park edges all year: Lands End, Fort Funston, the Presidio, Crissy Field and the west end of Golden Gate Park. Numbers rise sharply in winter.
species.photo: Males sing from the tops of coyote brush and lupine, which gives clean perches with distant backgrounds. The white crown stripes overexpose easily in sun, so watch the highlights. Winter flocks feeding on path edges are approachable at ground level.

species.ident: A large sparrow with a plain gray-brown face and breast, a dusky bill, and a yellow forecrown bordered by black, which is duller in winter. The song is a slow, descending series of three whistled notes.
species.nat: Winters in flocks, often mixed with White-crowned Sparrows, feeding on seeds, buds and flowers on the ground beside dense cover. Breeds in shrubby tundra and at treeline in Alaska and western Canada.
species.dist: A winter visitor throughout lowland and foothill California from late September to early May, most numerous near the coast.
species.find: Brushy park edges in winter: the Presidio, Golden Gate Park, Lands End, Glen Canyon Park and San Bruno Mountain.
species.photo: Available only in the cooler months, when the sun is low and the light is good for much of the day. The crown is brightest in April just before departure. Birds feeding on lawns at the edge of shrubs allow a low angle; 1/800 s handles normal feeding movement.

species.cons: Belding's race (south coast salt marsh) only: State Endangered

species.ident: A medium-sized, heavily streaked sparrow with a gray and brown striped face, long rounded tail and streaks that gather into a central breast spot. Bay Area birds are small and dark. Savannah Sparrow has a shorter notched tail and usually a yellowish eyebrow; Lincoln's Sparrow has finer streaks on a buff wash.
species.nat: Stays close to dense low vegetation, usually near water. Males sing a varied song beginning with a few clear notes from an exposed perch. Several subspecies are confined to the tidal marshes of San Francisco Bay.
species.dist: Resident through most of California in marshes, streamsides, coastal scrub and wet gardens; numbers increase in winter with migrants from the north.
species.find: Marsh edges and wet thickets: Heron's Head Park, Crissy Field marsh, Lake Merced, the Golden Gate Park lakes and Palo Alto Baylands.
species.photo: Singing males use the same reed or shrub top repeatedly through spring mornings; set up on a favored perch and wait. Reed stems confuse autofocus, so use a small zone or single point. A frame with the bill open in song needs about 1/1000 s.

species.ident: A large, plain, long-tailed sparrow, uniformly gray-brown with a rusty-buff throat ringed by faint dark streaks and warm cinnamon under the tail. The call is a sharp metallic 'chink'. Spotted Towhee is black, white and rufous; Abert's Towhee of the desert has a dark face.
species.nat: Forages on the ground, scratching in leaf litter with a two-footed hop for seeds and insects. Pairs stay together all year and keep in contact with a squealing duet. Nests low in dense shrubs.
species.dist: Resident in chaparral, coastal scrub, oak woodland edges and gardens through coastal and foothill California and Baja California; absent from the high mountains and deserts.
species.find: Easy to find along brushy edges and garden paths: the Presidio, Glen Canyon Park, McLaren Park, Lake Merced and Mount Davidson.
species.photo: Tame and ground-loving. Get low, near eye level with the bird, to blur the foreground and background; the brown plumage needs side light early or late in the day to show any texture. 1/500 s is enough for a feeding bird, 1/1000 s when it is scratching.
species.cons: Inyo race only: State Endangered; Federal Threatened

species.ident: A large sparrow with a black hood and upperparts (dark brown in females), white spots on the wings and back, rufous flanks, white belly and red eye. The song is a dry buzzy trill. California Towhee is plain brown.
species.nat: Scratches noisily in leaf litter under dense cover for insects, seeds and berries. Males sing from exposed shrub tops in spring. Nests on or near the ground.
species.dist: Resident through most of California in chaparral, coastal scrub, riparian thickets and forest understory, from the coast into the mountains. Some upslope birds move lower in winter.
species.find: Listen for the trill in coastal scrub and brushy canyons: Glen Canyon Park, the Presidio, San Bruno Mountain, Lands End and the Marin Headlands.
species.photo: Usually half-hidden, so the best chances are singing males on shrub tops in spring. The black hood and white belly are a high-contrast subject: expose for the whites and lift shadows later, and look for a catchlight in the red eye. Use a small AF zone to keep focus off intervening twigs.
